Question eight. What are precision, recall, and F one score? Precision: of everything flagged, the share that was right. Recall: of everything that was there, the share you caught. F one is their harmonic mean, high only when both are. In the page's eight examples, three caught, one missed and one false alarm: all three come to point seven five. On a real model they trade off along the threshold. Simulate a fraud model on a hundred thousand transactions, one percent fraud. At a threshold of point five, precision is eighty-four percent and recall twenty-four. At point one, thirty-five and fifty-four. Favor precision when false alarms are costly, recall when misses are: here, a false alarm blocks a good customer's card, and a miss loses the money. F one weighs them equally, which a business rarely does. Often capacity decides: if reviewers can check a thousand alerts a day, flag the top thousand. That catches four hundred and sixty-six of the nine hundred and ninety-five frauds.

Question nine. What is ar-oh-see ay-you-see, and when does pee-ar ay-you-see matter more? The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every threshold. Its area is the chance that a random positive is scored above a random negative. The fraud model's area is point nine one, which sounds strong. But the false positive rate divides by ninety-nine thousand legitimate transactions. At one percent, that's a thousand false alarms, nearly twice the frauds caught. The precision-recall curve never counts true negatives, so its area is what reviewers live with: point four six, against a chance level of point oh one, the fraud rate. When positives are rare, report pee-ar ay-you-see, and remember its baseline moves with the base rate.
